prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, Deep, Deuce

outputs.L1:
As phantoms direct life from the shadows, I feel as though I leaned against something, and it gave way beneath me. My father, on the porch with his crosswords, said, *this must be what it feels like to be dead.* When I returned from the dead, no one was there to greet me—yet still, you rejoice. I wander the ruins the way my tongue wanders my missing teeth; the brick and mortar of Deep Deuce have rotted like molars in an ancient mouth. Here, perhaps, Charlie Christian once walked.

The astrologer counseled patience and creative visualization: *Step One: Visualize an object that symbolizes the accursed influence. Picture yourself hurling it into a furnace. Step Two: Visualize the person responsible for the curse. Imagine a rope tied at one end around your waist, and at the other around theirs. See yourself severing it with a chainsaw as you cry out, "You have no power over me!" Step Three: Repeat twice daily for eleven days . . .*

You picture her green boots inside the furnace. No—you are standing in a crematorium, watching her body, perfect and corruptible, glide on its tray into the flame. Then you see yourself cutting the rope that binds you to her. And at last, your own corruptible and imperfect self—I mean, *me*—cries out, and I leap in after her.
outputs.L2: Unseen forces steer existence from the darkness, and I sense that whatever I depended upon has given way beneath me. Sitting on the porch with his crossword puzzle, my father remarked that this must resemble the sensation of death; Coming back from death, no one waited for me, yet you remain content— I trace the wreckage the way my tongue explores the gaps where teeth once were, the brick and mortar of Deep Deuce decayed like molars in some ancient jaw; This is ground Charlie Christian may have crossed— The astrologer advised patience alongside creative visualization: First: Picture an item representing the cursed force upon you. See yourself hurling it into a blazing furnace. Second: Envision the individual responsible for this curse. Imagine a cord binding your waist to theirs. See yourself severing that cord with a chainsaw while declaring, "You hold no power over me!" Third: Perform this ritual twice daily across eleven days . . . You picture her emerald boots consumed by flame . . . —No, wait. You're standing in a crematorium watching her flawless yet mortal form glide on a tray into the flames; Then you witness yourself sawing through the cord connecting you both; And finally your own flawed, mortal form—meaning myself—cries out and leaps in behind her.
outputs.L3:
# Fractured Ground

There is a particular quality to certain kinds of loss—not the clean grief of absence, but the disorienting sensation that the very architecture of one's being has given way. The speaker moves through this experience as though a load-bearing wall has cracked somewhere deep inside, and now everything that once stood upright leans at an unfamiliar angle. This is not merely sadness; it is structural. Something essential, something the self quietly depended upon without ever naming it, has buckled, and the aftermath is a kind of internal rubble that must be picked through, piece by piece, without any clear sense of what can be salvaged.

Death, in this context, becomes more than an ending—it becomes a metaphor stretched thin enough to cover the strange territory of feeling utterly alone even when surrounded by those who love you. To die and then return, in this figurative sense, is to walk back into a room full of familiar faces and discover that something in you no longer recognizes the warmth they offer. The isolation is not circumstantial; it is ontological. It follows the speaker like a shadow cast by an inner sun that has gone dark, so that even embrace, even presence, cannot fully reach the place where the alienation lives.

This inner collapse finds its echo in the outer world, specifically in the crumbling facades of Deep Deuce—a historic district whose walls have weathered decades, whose brick and mortar carry the accumulated weight of stories, music, and lives now gone. As the speaker observes this physical decay, it becomes impossible not to feel the body's own quiet betrayals mirrored there: the way skin loosens, the way strength ebbs, the way a place that once pulsed with vibrant communal life now stands hollowed, waiting. The personal and the historical fold into one another here—private deterioration and collective memory sharing the same crumbling foundation, each lending the other a deeper, more haunting resonance.

Against this backdrop of decay and disconnection, the speaker turns to ritual, as if seeking some mechanism—however desperate—to sever the curse that binds them to their suffering. The process unfolds with careful, almost liturgical precision: first, the visualization, conjuring the shape and texture of whatever invisible cord connects the speaker to their pain; then the fire, summoned not for destruction alone but for purification, a flame meant to consume the toxic residue of connection; and finally, the cutting—the symbolic severing of the rope that has, for so long, kept two fates entangled. Each step is performed with the gravity of someone who believes, or desperately wants to believe, that liberation is possible through careful, deliberate action.

And yet the ritual does not resolve as intended. Rather than achieving separation, the speaker finds the boundary between self and other dissolving in an unexpected direction. Instead of cutting free, they imagine crossing over—choosing to join the very figure they meant to release, drawn not toward liberation but toward reunion, however tragic. What begins as an act of severance transforms into an act of surrender, as the pull toward connection proves stronger than the promise of freedom. The curse, in the end, is not broken so much as reimagined, becoming something the speaker willingly walks into rather than escapes—a final, aching testament to how deeply loss and love remain entwined.
outputs.L4:
# Ashes on Deep Deuce

I.

The astrologer said: write his name on paper,
burn it beneath a waning moon,
watch the smoke carry the curse back
to whatever dark star birthed it.

She did not say what to do
with the smoke that looks like his hands.
She did not say what to do
when the smoke remembers how to hold you.

II.

Deep Deuce is rubble now—
brick teeth knocked out of Second Street,
the jazz halls swallowed by parking lots,
Ralph Ellison's ghost pacing where the Aldridge Theatre
used to spill light onto sidewalks
crowded with men who looked like my father
before he became a name I whisper
over kitchen matches.

My father's hands, that same brick color,
crumbling the same way—
mortar giving out between his knuckles
the year he stopped recognizing
his own reflection in store windows
that used to show him young.

III.

I write his name on the paper.
I write his name on the paper.
I write his name on the paper—
three times, because the ritual demands
a trinity, because grief
does not travel in straight lines
but circles back, circles back,
a moon that only knows how to wane
and then, cruelly, wax again.

IV.

Somewhere in the instructions
there is a line about release,
about watching the ash rise
and understanding: this is over.

But I have never been good
at understanding endings.
I held my father's hand
past the point when holding
stopped meaning anything to him.
I held my lover's face
in both palms the night before
he became someone I used to know,
memorizing the geography of his jaw
like a man memorizing his one
way out of a burning building.

V.

The paper curls. The name blackens.
For a moment I see him—
not my father, not exactly,
not my lover, not exactly—
some third body made of smoke
and matchlight and every street
that Deep Deuce used to be
before the city decided
memory was a kind of debt
best cleared with bulldozers.

The body in the fire turns.
It has his shoulders.
It has the shape of every door
that ever closed on me.

VI.

The instructions say: let it burn.
The instructions say: this is how
you sever what binds you.
The instructions say nothing
about the moment when the ash-body
turns to look at you
the way he used to look at you
across a kitchen table,
across a hospital bed,
across the wreckage of a neighborhood
that once held music in its bones.

VII.

I do not sever anything.

I reach into the flame.

I do not know if I am trying
to save him or follow him
or simply refuse, one final time,
the geometry of letting go—
the clean astrological arithmetic
that says a curse can be measured,
folded, burned, released
like something separate from the body
that first felt its weight.

VIII.

They will find the burns later
and ask what happened,
and I will not have language
for the leap into fire
after a shape made of smoke,
after a father, after a lover,
after a street that used to hold
saxophones and now holds
only silence and cracked foundations.

I will only be able to say:
I could not do the ritual right.
I could not release him.
I could not release any of them.

Grief does not sever.
It welds.

It takes the shape of your own hand
reaching into the fire,
and it does not let go,
and it does not let go,
and it does not let go.

# When Deep Meets Deuce

The tennis match had reached a critical juncture. The score stood at deuce, that peculiar moment in tennis when both players have won three points each, forcing the game into a heightened state of tension. Every point from here would matter more than the last, as one player would need to win two consecutive points to claim the game.

Sarah stood at the baseline, breathing deeply, trying to find her center. When the pressure mounted like this, she had learned to focus on something deeper than technique—a mental discipline that went beyond the physical mechanics of her serve or forehand.

Her coach had always said that deuce moments reveal character. When the score is even and everything hangs in the balance, players discover how deep their resolve truly runs. It's not about who has the better shots in that instant, but who can dig deeper into their reserves of concentration and composure.

The rally that followed was intense. Deep groundstrokes from both sides, each player trying to push the other behind the baseline. When Sarah finally saw an opening—a short ball that landed shallow in the court—she moved forward decisively, ending the point with a crisp volley.

Advantage Sarah. But she knew from experience that deuce could return again in an instant, as it so often does in matches that go deep into competitive territory. The mental game, she reminded herself, was just as important as the physical one. When athletes learn to embrace these pressure-filled moments rather than fear them, they discover a deeper reservoir of skill and determination they never knew existed.

The next point would tell the story, as it always does when a match teeters on this delicate edge between triumph and continued struggle.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem that blends grief over a lost parent with imagery of Deep Deuce and jazz history, ending in a surreal act of self-sacrifice.
counterfactuals.output:
# Deep Deuce Elegy

My father died in the key of B-flat, somewhere between Second Street and the memory of horns. I walked Deep Deuce looking for him in the brick facades, in the ghosted marquees where Christine still sang and the Blue Devils still stomped their feet against a Tuesday that no longer exists. The historical marker doesn't mention grief. It doesn't say *here is where a daughter comes to lose herself in what was lost before her, doubling the loss like a chord progression that never resolves.*

I inherited his hands—not the shape of them, but the way they'd curl around a phantom trumpet when he thought no one watched. He used to say Oklahoma City was a jazz town before it was anything else, before the highway cut through and swallowed half the clubs whole. He said Ralph Ellison walked these same streets as a boy, listening. I think grief is a kind of listening too—the ear pressed to a door that will never open again, straining for a bassline underneath the silence.

Now I go there at dusk when the light turns the color of old photographs, amber and forgetting. I sit on the curb where the Aldridge Theater used to hold whole galaxies of sound, and I take my own ribs apart like a musician disassembling a horn for cleaning. One by one, I lay them on the sidewalk—bone by bone, a xylophone of myself. This is not destruction. This is devotion.

I climb inside the empty space where my heart was and I become the instrument my father always wanted: hollow enough to hold a note, hollow enough to be filled with someone else's breath. The wind moves through my open chest and it sounds like Charlie Christian tuning up, like every horn player who ever left this street humming in the marrow.

I let the night play me. I let Deep Deuce remember itself through the reed of my sternum. Somewhere in this surrender, my father exhales through what's left of me, one long low note that finally, finally resolves—

and I become the song that carries him home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a fragmented, stream-of-consciousness poem mixing memories of a father, references to Charlie Christian, and an astrologer's ritual for breaking a curse.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salt on the Windowsill**

my father's hands smelled like guitar strings and Lucky Strikes
*Solo Flight* spinning on the hi-fi, 1941 bleeding into
the kitchen, 1979, he'd say *listen to that boy play*
Charlie Christian dead at twenty-five and still
teaching my father's fingers how to grieve

the astrologer said burn the photograph at midnight
but which midnight, which father, which
version of him standing in the doorway not leaving
not staying, Mercury retrograde in his blood
since the day he was born under a curse he didn't choose

*I found my thrill* — no wait, that's someone else's song
my father hummed it wrong, always wrong,
off-key like the moon in the eighth house
she said *bury salt where he last stood*
but he never stood still long enough to leave a mark

Charlie's amplifier crackling through the Sherman Hotel
1939 or was it my father's transistor radio
static and swing tangled together in my chest
the astrologer's candles, seven of them,
seven years since I've said his name out loud

*this is a picture of a man mid-solo, mid-sentence*
*this is a curse I inherited like perfect pitch*

she says the ritual requires three things:
his handwriting, his blood-name, salt water from a place
he never visited — I have none of these
only a chord progression I can't resolve
only Charlie's guitar bending notes that shouldn't exist
only my father's cough in another room, 1985,
the smoke curling up like something trying to leave the body

break the curse she says means
stop playing the same four bars over
but grief is a jazz standard, it repeats
with variation, with feeling, with
my father's ghost soloing through my own hands now

Saturn returns and I am my father's age
holding a guitar I don't know how to play
listening to a dead man improvise
against a curse none of us asked for
salt scattered, unswept, on every windowsill I've owned
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental poetry that juxtaposes a numbered "curse-breaking" visualization exercise with a personal narrative about mourning and returning "from the dead."
counterfactuals.output:
# Instructions for Breaking a Family Curse (Visualization, with Interruptions)

**1.** Sit comfortably. Close your eyes. Picture the curse as a black thread running through your grandmother's hands, your mother's hands, your hands.

*The morning she died I was folding laundry. I did not know yet that a body could just stop, the way a sentence stops when you forget what you were saying.*

**2.** Follow the thread backward through three generations. Do not flinch when it tightens.

*I flinched. I have always flinched. It is, perhaps, the one thing I inherited cleanly.*

**3.** Locate the knot. It will be warm, or cold, or nothing at all — trust whatever you feel.

*I felt nothing for four months. Then I felt everything at once in a grocery store, over a bin of lemons she used to buy by the dozen for no reason anyone could explain.*

**4.** Speak the knot's name aloud. If you don't know its name, name it anyway. This is allowed.

*Her name was Marion. I keep almost writing "is."*

**5.** Visualize a pair of scissors made of light.

*The doctors said six minutes without a pulse. I don't remember the six minutes. I remember before, and I remember a hallway that smelled like the inside of a mouth, and I remember being furious that I had come back at all.*

**6.** Cut the thread. It will not hurt. This is a lie you must believe for the exercise to work.

**6.** *(repeat)* It did hurt. Everything that survives hurts on the way back in — blood into fingers, grief into a body that thought it was finished being a body.

**7.** Watch the severed ends fall away like something molting.

*I molted in a hospital gown. I molted at the funeral, in the wrong shoes. I molted again just now, writing this, shedding a version of myself that still thinks silence is the same as peace.*

**8.** Notice: you are still standing. The curse does not know this yet.

*I am still standing. My mother is not. There is no visualization for that asymmetry — no scissors, no light, no numbered step that puts a person back inside her own hands.*

**9.** Breathe. Say: *I am the one who lived.* Say it until it stops sounding like an accusation.

*I am the one who lived.*
*I am the one who lived.*
*I am the—*

**7.** *(again, out of order, because grief does not go in order)*
Watch the severed ends fall away.

*She is not falling away. She is a thread still running through my hands, warm, uncut, refusing every scissors of light I have ever imagined.*

**10.** Open your eyes. The curse is broken. Notice how ordinary the room looks.

*The room looks ordinary. There is a coffee cup. There is my own pulse, absurd and continuing. There is the lemon on the counter I bought for no reason anyone could explain.*

**11.** If you feel nothing, that is normal. The body keeps its own ledger of what it survived, and pays it out slowly, in installments, for the rest of your life.

*I am still paying.*
*I have started calling this living.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting literary passage about walking through the ruins of a historic African American neighborhood while processing loss, incorporating instructions from a psychic or astrologer.
counterfactuals.output:
The astrologer had told her to walk at dusk, when the veil between what-was and what-remains grows thin as onion skin. *Go to the place that was erased,* she'd said, shuffling cards that meant nothing and everything. *Walk it like a prayer. Bring something you're willing to leave behind.*

So Odessa drove out to Rosewood-that-was, or the patch of Florida scrubland that used to answer to that name, and left her car at the edge of a road that dissolved into weeds. The GPS had no opinion about where she was going. Some places refuse to be mapped twice.

She carried her grandmother's funeral program folded in her coat pocket, soft now from handling, the photograph gone gray at the edges like something remembering itself into fog. The astrologer said to bring something willing to be left. She wasn't sure yet if this qualified.

The land here held its history the way scar tissue holds a wound—smoothed over, but different from the skin around it. A chimney stood alone in a clearing, its house long since taken by fire or time or the particular violence that erases a people twice: once by flame, once by forgetting. She touched the brick and it was warm, though the sun had already dropped behind the pines, and she told herself that was just the day's heat leaving slowly, the way grief does, the way anything does that doesn't want to go.

*You will feel them,* the astrologer had promised, *not as ghosts but as arrangement—the way birds arrange themselves before a storm, the way your body knows a room has been recently occupied.*

And she did feel it: a thickness in the air where a porch might have been, the ghost-geometry of streets that existed only in deed books and the memory of the very old. Here, perhaps, a church. Here, a schoolhouse where children conjugated verbs into a future someone decided they wouldn't have. The dusk moved through the palmettos, and the palmettos did not so much rustle as *sigh*, an old syllable, worn smooth by too many years of being the only witness.

She thought of her grandmother, three weeks gone now, whose body had returned to earth the way this town had returned to weeds—not erased, exactly, but requiring excavation. Requiring someone to come at dusk with their pockets full of paper and grief and stand very still until the land agreed to speak.

*Leave the thing,* the astrologer's voice returned to her, insistent as a held note. *Not to forget. To plant.*

Odessa knelt where she guessed a threshold might have been—there was a slight rise in the earth, stubborn as memory—and dug with her fingers until the sandy soil gave way. She placed the funeral program in the hollow, folded now into something like a seed, something like a door. She covered it over. The dark had fully come by then, and the first stars did what stars do, indifferent and burning, the same light that had witnessed everything here and said nothing, the same sky Rosewood's dead had watched go dark a hundred years before.

She did not feel forgiveness. She had not come for forgiveness. She had come, she understood now, the way water comes to low ground—not by choice, but by the shape of what's missing.

Somewhere in the dark, something long extinguished continued, quietly, to grow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, emotionally raw poem where instructions for exorcising a curse gradually merge with a scene of cremation and the speaker's own act of self-destruction.
counterfactuals.output:
**Rite for the Body That Would Not Leave**

First, you must find the hour before dawn
when the mouth of the house still holds its breath.
Salt the doorframe. Salt the tongue.
Speak the name backward until it forgets
what it was called when it was loved.

Light something. It doesn't matter what—
paper, hair, the letters you kept
folded like small coffins in a drawer.
The smoke will rise the way smoke always rises,
indifferent, the way grief is indifferent
to the shape it wears out of you.

Now the body on the pyre—
is it his, is it yours, is it the thing
that lived between your ribs
wearing your face to dinner parties?
The instructions say: *do not weep upon the ash.*
The instructions do not say what to do
when the ash is already inside your throat,
has been inside your throat since the beginning,
since before you knew there was a beginning.

Draw the circle. Draw it again.
Your hand is shaking because your hand
knows something your mind refuses—
that the curse and the cure
are wearing each other's clothes,
that the flame eating the corpse
is the same flame you are feeding
piece by piece, finger by finger,
into your own open sternum.

*Command it to leave in the name of—*
in the name of what, exactly.
The fire doesn't care what god you invoke.
It only wants to be finished eating.
It only wants what you want:
to stop being the haunted house
and become, instead, the clean field after,
the black grass, the silence
that isn't peace but is at least quiet.

Third instruction: *anoint the threshold with ash.*
You are the threshold now.
You are the ash and the hand holding it
and the wind deciding where you'll land.

Somewhere the pyre collapses inward,
a soft architecture giving up its shape.
Somewhere your ribs do the same—
not broken, just finally admitting
they were never load-bearing,
were only ever holding the shape
of something that wanted out.

Last instruction, the one no one writes down:
when the fire finishes both bodies—
the one on the pyre, the one that lit it—
do not look for what remains.
There is no triumphant spirit
rising clean into morning.
There is only smoke, dispersing,
which was always the closest thing
you had to a soul,
and the field, black and steaming,
which was always the closest thing
you had to a self,
and the quiet after,
which you must now learn to call
survival,
though it sounds, in your mouth,
exactly like an ending.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
